title: overlay.py and profile.py have no tests
description:
Neither module has a direct test. Both are on the main path: the overlay is the one artifact an operator hand-edits, and profiling decides every string width in the replica.

The correlation is worth naming. Every defect this review turned up sits on a path with no test, and the two untested modules are where several of them are.

Specific gaps:

- `write_overlay_stub` output is never round-tripped through `load_overlay` and `apply_overlay`, so nothing checks that what `infer` writes is what the overlay reader accepts. Column names containing YAML-special characters would break the unquoted flow lists the stub emits.
- `apply_overlay`'s merge and replace modes, `add_tables`, and the warning paths are unexercised.
- Profiling has no test of batching, the sampling wrapper, or `profile_warnings`.
- `test_closed_interval_changes_boundary` asserts that a string appears in generated text; it would pass with the boundary logic inverted.
- The read-only engine guard and the `information_schema` parsing are both untested.

## Done when

The overlay round-trips from stub to applied spec in a test, both merge modes and the warning paths are covered, profiling is exercised against SQLite or a fake, and the closed-interval test runs a query instead of reading text.
close_reason: tests/test_overlay.py and tests/test_profile.py, 39 tests. Writing them found the unquoted stub flow sequences and the rejected-only table emitting a bare key, both fixed alongside.

title: Validation and profiling SQL only runs on Databricks
description:
Every statement `infer --validate` and `profile` build is a Databricks-flavoured f-string: `LIMIT` for sampling, backtick quoting through `quote_ident`, `LENGTH()`, and three-part catalog-qualified names from `qualify()`. None of that runs on SQL Server, which uses `TOP`, bracket quoting, `LEN()`, and a different qualification shape.

Nothing depends on this today, because both commands only ever point at the source catalog. It becomes a precondition the moment anything wants to run the same checks against a second copy of the data - which is what any data-driven candidate generation would need, and what the second binding exists for in every other part of the tool.

The generated model layer already solves this problem: one class hierarchy, generic types with `mssql` variants, and a schema token that resolves per engine. The inference and profiling SQL is the one place that reaches for the source dialect directly.

## Two routes

Build the statements as SQLAlchemy Core selects against the spec, letting the dialect compile them, which is the same answer `replica_ddl` already uses for DDL. Or keep the f-strings and gate the dialect-specific fragments behind the engine's dialect name.

The first is more work and matches how the rest of the tool addresses two backends. The second is smaller and leaves a second dialect-shaped decision in the code for the next person.

## Done when

`infer --validate` and `profile` produce statements that run against either backend, and a test asserts the compiled form for both rather than only the Databricks one.

title: Foreign key target index lets one table claim a key name used in several schemas
description:
`propose_foreign_keys` builds one flat index of key names for the whole spec and populates it with `targets.setdefault(name, (tbl, keys[0]))`. The index is keyed by normalised name only — `_key_names(table_name)` plus the parent's own primary key column name — with no schema component, while table identity everywhere else in the spec is `schema.name`.

So when two schemas both contain a table of the same name, whichever is reached first in `spec.primary_tables` claims every name it generates. A second `Customer` in another schema registers nothing, and every `CustomerId` column in every schema is proposed against the first one. `setdefault` makes this silent: no warning, no lowered score, and the proposal reads exactly like a correct one at 0.80 with "types agree".

Single-schema runs cannot hit this. It appears the first time several schemas are introspected together, which is also the only way cross-schema foreign keys are found at all, so it arrives precisely when the feature starts being used.

## Options

- Key the index by schema and prefer a same-schema parent, falling back to another schema only when the name is unique across the spec.
- Detect the collision and emit both proposals at a reduced score with the ambiguity named in the reason, leaving the choice to the overlay.
- Detect the collision and emit neither, with a warning naming the competing tables.

The second and third keep the resolution in the operator's hands, which matches how the rest of inference treats things it cannot settle from names alone. The first is a guess that will be right often enough to be trusted and wrong without saying so.

## Done when

Two same-named tables in different schemas cannot silently capture each other's child columns, and `tests/test_pipeline.py` covers a spec with the collision in it.
close_reason: The target index maps a name to every table claiming it. A parent in the child's own schema settles the match; with none, every candidate is proposed at half score with the rivals named, and to_foreign_key_specs drops a column two parents claim rather than choosing.

title: Resolve schema tokens at compile time
description:
SQLAlchemy resolves a `schema_translate_map` during a standalone compile when asked. `stmt.compile(dialect=..., schema_translate_map=m, render_schema_translate=True)` renders real schema names with no engine and no connection.

Three places in this repo state the opposite: the docstring on `replica_ddl`, the bindings page under "How the schema token works", and the schema mapping section of the ddl page. `replica_ddl` also clones every table into a fresh `MetaData` to work around a limitation that is not there.

Checked against SQLAlchemy 2.0.52 with the mssql dialect: an ORM select renders `stele__dbo.[Widget]` without the flag and `[ReplicaDb_dbo].[Widget]` with it, `CreateTable` renders the same way, and a history `as_of` select compiles standalone carrying its interval predicate with literal binds.

## Binding.compile

`Binding.compile(stmt, *, literal_binds=False) -> Compiled` renders a statement for the binding's dialect with the binding's schema names. `str(compiled)` is the SQL, `compiled.params` the values in the dialect's paramstyle, and `literal_binds` renders values into the text for consumers that accept SQL alone. A token the map does not name renders as itself, which is what execution does too.

This is the one thing a consumer outside SQLAlchemy lacks. Anything taking SQL text - a warehouse SQL API, another engine, a dataframe reader that unwraps to a raw cursor - otherwise receives the token.

**Implementation note.** Request rendering only when the map is non-empty. The compiler asserts a map is present when rendering is requested, so a binding constructed with no schemas raises a bare `AssertionError` otherwise. Confirmed.

## replica_ddl

Build the token map from the logical mapping and compile each `CreateTable` with it rendered. The `MetaData` clone and the `referred_schema_fn` go away. Foreign key targets render through the same preparer.

One behavioural difference to settle deliberately rather than by accident: the current code also maps schemas that are not tokens, and the render path leaves those alone.

## Docs

Two corrections and one new section, all on `docs/generated/index.md` and `docs/pipeline/ddl-and-check.md`.

The corrections: both pages state that a standalone compile shows the token and cannot resolve it. Both are wrong and both change. The bindings page's debugging example becomes `binding.compile(stmt)`.

The new section is worked Python, not a signature. Someone who has only read the bindings page should be able to write the calls without inventing anything:

- A select against generated classes, compiled for a binding, showing the rendered SQL with real schema names in the output. Show the same statement compiled for the other binding so the point of the exercise - one statement, two backends, two schema names - is on the page rather than implied.
- Both handoff forms, and when each applies: `str(compiled)` with `compiled.params` for a consumer that binds parameters itself, and `literal_binds=True` for one that takes a complete statement and nothing else.
- A history select, `History.as_of(ts)`, compiled standalone with its interval predicate rendered. This is the case that earns the method: the point-in-time logic travels into the SQL, so whatever receives it is correctly filtered without reimplementing the predicate.

Three behaviours the examples state rather than leave to be discovered: a statement compiled and handed elsewhere leaves the session behind, so a pinned session does not narrow it and the statement carries its own instant; a token the map does not name renders as itself; a binding with no schemas compiles without translation.

The page also shows the four-line equivalent using `stmt.compile()` with `dialect`, `schema_translate_map` and `render_schema_translate` directly, and says the method is a wrapper over it. The wrapper exists for the empty-map case, which raises a bare `AssertionError`, and for discoverability - not because the underlying call is unavailable.

## Done when

`Binding.compile` is typed and tested on both dialects, including a history `as_of` select with literal binds and a binding with no schemas; `replica_ddl` has no clone and its DDL test passes unchanged; the three false statements are corrected; and the bindings page carries runnable examples covering both handoff forms and the history case, with `mkdocs build --strict` passing.
close_reason: Binding.compile added with worked examples; replica_ddl no longer clones; the three false statements corrected

title: Keep dependencies and workflows updated with Dependabot and audited with zizmor
description:
Two supply-chain gaps: nothing proposes dependency or GitHub Actions updates, and nothing checks the workflows for the usual Actions security mistakes.

Add `.github/dependabot.yml` covering the `uv` ecosystem (`pyproject.toml` plus `uv.lock`) and `github-actions`, both weekly with a 7-day cooldown so a release has to survive a week before it is proposed. Group each ecosystem into a single pull request so a week of updates is one review rather than five.

Add `zizmor` to the dev dependency group and a step to `check.sh`, so workflow auditing runs locally and in CI through the same script as every other check. Fix what it reports on the existing workflow: pin both actions to commit hashes with the version in a trailing comment, set `persist-credentials: false` on checkout, and declare explicit `permissions`.

Action versions stay where they are; Dependabot proposes the major bumps on its own schedule.
close_reason: Dependabot config and zizmor step landed; workflow findings fixed

title: Document the pipeline and the generated package in a Material for MkDocs guide
description:
The README is the only documentation, and it carries two jobs badly: it is the first thing a reader sees, and it is also the step-by-step reference for a six-command pipeline. It should keep the first job and hand off the second. Nothing at all covers using the package that comes out, and the least guessable parts are the ones a reader cannot recover from the emitted code.

## Why Material for MkDocs

Markdown sources beside the code, a navigation tree, and code-block rendering with tabs for the Databricks and SQL Server sides of the same example. The alternative is growing the README until it stops being readable in a terminal, which it is currently sized for.

## What the README keeps

An introduction and an overview: what the tool is for, the shape of catalog it assumes, the `model.yaml` / `overlay.yaml` split as the central design idea, the six commands as a diagram, install, and a pointer to the guide. Everything below "Walkthrough" moves.

## What the guide covers

**Overview and setup.** What the tool assumes about a catalog and why. Install, connection settings and their precedence, and a first run end to end against one schema.

**The pipeline, one page per command.** `introspect`, `profile`, `infer`, `generate`, `ddl`, `check`. Each page says what the command reads, what it writes, and which flags change the outcome rather than the presentation.

**What the code actually looks for.** This is the section with no existing equivalent, and the reason someone would trust or distrust the output.

- Introspection: the four `information_schema` queries, the Inspector fallback and when it fires, how `X` is paired with `X_history` and how the history table's key is derived.
- Profiling: what is sampled, why an observed maximum is a lower bound on a declared width, and why lengths are rounded up to buckets.
- Primary key inference: the three rules in order — a key affix on either side of the table name, a bare generic name in a leading position, a stem match — with the scores each produces and the bonuses for non-nullable and leading ordinal.
- Foreign key inference: how candidate names are built, that a parent needs a single-column key to be a target, how a parent in the child's own schema settles a contested name, and what happens when none does.
- Validation: what `--validate` counts, and how containment and null fraction turn a name match into evidence.
- The score table, and what `--min-score` does at each threshold.

**Changing the output.** Where each kind of correction belongs: introspection flags for SCD2 shape, `--include` and `--exclude` for scope, `type_override` for widths, and the overlay for keys, relationships, names, and tables the catalog never reported. The rule that `model.yaml` and `models/` are regenerable and the overlay is not.

**Gotchas.** Every schema must be introspected together for cross-schema relationships to be found. `infer` never reads the overlay. `infer` will not overwrite an existing overlay without `--force`. `profile` and `infer` have no schema filter. Composite keys are not proposed. Self-references are not auto-proposed. Complex types do not round-trip.

**Using the generated package.** Binding, the schema token and `schema_translate_map`, one query against both backends, and why Databricks opens read-only.

**Joins and history, worked.** Examples against a model with enough shape to be worth reading: several schemas, a table whose key names run the other way, two tables sharing a name across schemas, a composite key declared by hand, and a history pair. Cover the `history` relationship, each SCD2 helper including what `current` does when the live row is not duplicated into history, and the hand-written join a history class needs because it carries no relationships of its own — see [[bd-nzy]].

**What the types tell you.** What carries the element type through and what stays open, each for a stated reason.

## Decisions this needs

- Whether the docs build runs in CI. A job that fails on a broken link is worth more than the docs themselves.
- Whether examples are executed. `examples/demo_sqlite.py` already runs a full SCD2 story against SQLite; sourcing snippets from a file the tests execute keeps the guide from drifting, which the README's snippets cannot do.

## Done when

A Material for MkDocs site builds from `docs/`, covers the sections above, and the README is back to introduction and overview with a pointer to it.
close_reason: docs/ builds with Material for MkDocs and covers overview, setup, one page per command, the full heuristic and scoring rules, where each kind of correction belongs, gotchas, and the generated package: bindings and schema translation, relationships, history, and typing. README reduced to overview plus a first run. check.sh builds the docs with --strict.

title: SCD2 query helpers return Select[Any], erasing the element type
description:
`HistoryMixin.as_of`, `current`, `changes_between`, and `versions_of` are all annotated `-> Select[Any]`, as is `as_of_all`. Each one returns `select(cls)` or a filtered form of it, so the element type is known at the point of construction and thrown away by the annotation.

The effect is that the typing on `Binding.scalars` and `Binding.rows` does not reach the queries most callers actually write. `binding.scalars(select(Customer))` resolves to `list[Customer]`, but `binding.scalars(CustomerHistory.as_of(ts))` resolves to `list[Any]`, because `Any` satisfies the `Select[tuple[T]]` parameter with `T` bound to `Any`. No error is raised; the type is simply gone. The generated SCD2 helpers are the main query surface, so this is the path that matters.

The fix is `Select[tuple[Self]]` on the classmethods, `dict[str, Select[tuple[HistoryMixin]]]` or a generic equivalent for `as_of_all`. `versions_of` takes `entity: Any` as well, which is a separate and smaller question.

This carries the same SQLAlchemy version constraint as the `Binding` signatures: the one-tuple spelling is a 2.0 form, and 2.1 makes `Select` variadic. The decision recorded on the `Binding` work applies here unchanged — use the 2.0 spelling, add no upper bound, and let a mypy error be the signal if 2.1 ever gets installed.

## Done when

The point-in-time helpers carry the element type, and a test asserts the inferred type with `typing.assert_type` the way `tests/test_binding_types.py` does.
close_reason: as_of, changes_between, versions_of and timeline return Select[tuple[Self]]. current keeps Select[tuple[Any]] because it selects the primary table when current_in_history is false, so the element class is a property of the model rather than the call. as_of_all keeps Any: a type variable there names the element type only for a single-class list and rejects the mixed list it exists for.

title: Document a repository layout around the generated package
description:
Nothing says how to lay out a repository around the four pipeline artifacts, and it is the first question after a first run. The answer follows from one rule: **every regenerable file is committed, and CI proves it is regenerable.**

Committing `model.yaml` is what makes `generate`, `ddl` and `check` credential-free for every contributor and every offline CI run. Only `introspect`, `profile` and `infer --validate` need the catalog.

## The page

`docs/repository.md`, in the nav after "Changing the output". It shows one layout: `model.yaml` and `overlay.yaml` at the root where the CLI defaults already find them, the generated package under `src/` with a name the user picks, the user's own code in a sibling package, `replica.sql` at the root, `.env` ignored.

Every stele invocation goes in one recipe - a `Makefile` target or `justfile` recipe - that people and CI both call, so no CI workflow carries a stele flag and nothing in the page's workflow snippet can rot into a wrong command.

Two jobs, shown for one provider and described so they transfer:

- **Offline, every push.** Run the recipe, then fail if the working tree is dirty. `git status --porcelain` rather than `git diff --exit-code`, because a new table produces an untracked file that `git diff` does not see. This is what makes "never hand-edited" true rather than aspirational.
- **Scheduled and credentialed.** Run `introspect`, and `profile` on a slower cadence; if `model.yaml` moved, regenerate and open a pull request. Never `infer --force` on a schedule - the pull request names any new tables and a person runs `infer` for them.

## What the page states plainly

The generated package changes when stele changes, so a stele upgrade regenerates it with no catalog change at all - otherwise the first dependency bump looks like a mystery failure.

`profile --sample N` is a `LIMIT` with no `ORDER BY`, so the sample differs between runs. Lengths are bucketed, so most runs show nothing, but a bucket crossing is a real widening.

The scheduled job holds a long-lived personal access token, because the connection settings accept nothing else.

## What the page must not do

Prescribe a CI provider beyond one worked example, show a stele flag outside the recipe, or claim the diff job catches hand-edits to `overlay.yaml`. The overlay is an input; nothing regenerates it.

## Not a subcommand

A scaffolding command was considered and rejected, including the version that delegates to `uv` rather than writing a project skeleton itself. That version is the stronger one: `uv init --package`, `uv add stele`, then only the stele-specific files. It is still not worth building.

Most of what such a command would produce is unknowable to stele - the CI provider, the schedule, the secret names, which schemas, whether anything consumes `replica.sql`. The piece with the most value is the CI workflow, which `uv` does not emit and whose action pins go stale the day they are written. Delegation also buys a dependency: stele installs and runs without `uv` today, and a subcommand shelling out to it would make `uv` a runtime requirement of that path, against a CLI that is still moving.

The check the command would exist to set up needs no stele logic in any case. `generate` is deterministic given the two files, so proving the committed package matches them is "regenerate, then look at the tree".

There is a middle option if adoption ever outgrows one person: a template repository, cloned rather than generated. It is executable rather than inert, its own CI proves it works on every push, and it needs no code in stele and no `uv` coupling. The cost is a second repository to keep in step with stele's output. This page is what such a template would be built from, so it comes first either way.

## Done when

The page exists and is in the nav, `mkdocs build --strict` passes, and the pipeline overview links to it from its credentials table.
close_reason: docs/repository.md written, in the nav, linked from the pipeline overview and the reading list

title: Rough edges in generated code and around the CLI
description:
A grab bag from a review pass, none individually urgent.

**Generated code**, against the stated bar of reading like hand-written SQLAlchemy: `ForeignKey` is imported into every module whether used or not, and the template always imports `HistoryMixin`, `SCD2Config` and `TYPE_CHECKING`, so a module without history fails a lint someone points at it. Three blank lines after imports when there is no `TYPE_CHECKING` block, one blank line between the primary and history classes. Composite primaryjoins render a space before the comma.

**Runtime:** two functions named `utcnow` with different signatures, and the exported one - `history.utcnow(cfg)` - is not the one `Binding` uses, so a user calling the documented export with no argument gets a `TypeError`. Calling `pin()` twice on one session stacks listeners and duplicates criteria.

**Dead code:** `types.ceil_pow2`, `ColumnSpec.python_name`, and a `bucket_length` call in `profile.py` whose result is discarded.

**CLI:** `ddl --schema` values without `=` traceback. `check` and `ddl` require the package directory's basename to be a valid module name. `naive_utc` is the only `HistoryConfig` setting with no introspect flag, and nothing says so. An `--include` pattern matching `X` but not `X_history` silently drops versioning.

**Inference and overlay details:** three different `min_score` defaults across `infer()`, `apply_to_spec` and the CLI. `infer()` mutates the caller's spec as an undocumented side effect, which also makes `--apply`'s count wrong. An unknown `foreign_keys_mode` silently behaves as merge. `spec_version` is written and never checked. A lowercase `type_override` emits an import of the literal type name and fails at check.

**Profiling:** an all-empty-string column profiles as length 0 and becomes `NVARCHAR(MAX)` with a note telling you to run the profile you just ran. The Inspector fallback drops views while the information_schema path keeps them, with nothing saying so.

**Docs drift:** `ddl-and-check.md`'s sample DDL shows unnamed constraints where the naming convention emits named ones. `pipeline/generate.md` says the output directory is overwritten, but stale modules from a previous run are left in place.
close_reason: generated code lints clean, the runtime duplicates are gone, the CLI reports what it used to traceback on, and the shared defaults agree

title: introspect stamps the run time, so two runs against an unchanged catalog differ
description:
`introspect` records `generated_at` in the spec, and `generate` copies it into the generated package docstring. A repository that commits `model.yaml` and re-runs `introspect` on a schedule therefore sees a diff on every run, and has to filter that line out to tell drift from noise.

Git already records when a file changed, so the field carries nothing the history does not.

## Two routes

Stop writing it: `introspect` omits the field, the template stops rendering the line, and a spec regenerated from an unchanged catalog is byte-identical to the committed one. Or keep it and document `git diff -I` as the comparison for anyone diffing the file.

The first is the smaller rule, and it is what makes "regenerate and check the tree is clean" work without an exception. `source`, which names the host and catalog, stays: it does not vary between runs and it says what the file describes.

## Done when

Two `introspect` runs against one unchanged spec fixture produce identical files, the generated package header no longer carries the line, and any test reading that header is updated.
close_reason: generated_at removed from the spec, introspect and the package header; a dumped spec round-trips byte-identical

title: Write a prior-art page relating stele to existing tools and research
description:
stele derives its heuristics and its file layout from first principles, and nobody has checked whether the same problems are already solved elsewhere. Two risks follow: reinventing something worse than what exists, and failing to credit work the design is effectively built on.

The deliverable is a documentation page - `docs/prior-art.md` or similar - saying how stele relates to existing tools and research. Not a defensive comparison table; a short honest account of what is solved elsewhere, what stele borrows, and what it does differently and why.

## The bar for citations

Every claim about another project must be checked against that project's own documentation or source, and the page must say which. "Its README states" and "reading its source shows" are different claims and should read differently. Anything inferred rather than verified is either checked or cut - a prior-art page that misdescribes a neighbouring project is worse than no page.

## The six capabilities to research

Each is a separate question with its own literature.

**Generating SQLAlchemy models from a live database.** SQLAlchemy's own `automap`, `sqlacodegen`, the older `sqlautocode`. Also worth a look for shape rather than language: Django `inspectdb`, Prisma introspection, JOOQ's generator, Hibernate reverse engineering.

**Inferring keys and references when the catalog declares none.** This is the axis most likely to have real prior art, and it has both tools and an academic literature. Unique column combination discovery and inclusion dependency discovery are the formal names; Metanome is the best-known research platform, and HyFD, Sindy and Binder are algorithms worth reading about even if no usable implementation exists. Find out whether the containment measure stele uses has a standard name and a standard threshold.

**Recovering string widths by profiling.** Great Expectations, ydata-profiling, and whatever the data-quality world uses for the same job.

**SCD2 query helpers in an ORM.** `sqlalchemy-continuum`, `sqlalchemy-history`, SQL:2011 system-versioned tables, Postgres temporal extensions. The specific question is whether any of them attaches to history tables that already exist in a source system with their own start and end columns, rather than managing tables it created itself.

**One model set addressing two backends.** SQLAlchemy's `schema_translate_map` is the mechanism stele uses; the question is whether anyone else builds a generator on it.

**The regenerate-plus-overlay pattern.** dbt's `schema.yml`, SQLMesh, Terraform's split between configuration and state, OpenAPI and protobuf generator customisation layers. Whether this shape has a name is itself worth knowing.

## What is already established

Two fetches were made before the session's web search budget ran out. Both are grounded in the projects' own documentation.

**`sqlacodegen` stops where stele starts.** It generates declarative SQLAlchemy 2.x from a live database and relies on existing database constraints: its documentation states it does not infer missing primary or foreign keys. A table with no primary key degrades to a bare `Table` rather than a mapped class. There is no customisation layer surviving regeneration and no profiling. On a federated catalog that declares nothing, it produces almost nothing - which is the input stele exists for. Source: https://github.com/agronholm/sqlacodegen

**`sqlalchemy-continuum` is unresolved and should not be summarised from what was read.** Its documentation index confirms a versioning extension that manages its own version and transaction tables and offers querying entities at a given revision. Whether it can attach to pre-existing SCD2 tables with their own interval columns - the only question that matters here - is not answerable from the index. The Basics and Configuration pages settle it. Source: https://sqlalchemy-continuum.readthedocs.io/en/latest/

## Method

Do this single-threaded. Fanning it across five agents exhausted a 200-call web search budget without producing a report, and the budget is per session: check `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION` before starting, and spend searches on discovery rather than on re-reading pages already known.

## Done when

A page exists that states, per capability, what already exists and how close it is, with every citation checked and its basis named. Anything that turns out to be solved elsewhere is said plainly, including if the honest conclusion is that some part of stele should be replaced by an existing tool.
close_reason: docs/prior-art.md covers the six capabilities, every citation checked against the project's own docs or source, unverifiable leads named as such

## Read these three first (about four hours)

1. Abedjan, Golab, Naumann. Profiling relational data: a survey. The VLDB Journal 24(4): 557-581, 2015. doi:10.1007/s00778-015-0389-y. Free PDF: https://hpi.de/fileadmin/user_upload/fachgebiete/naumann/publications/2015/dataprofiling_main.pdf — Read section 2 (task classification), 5.1 (UCCs and keys), 5.3 including 5.3.5 "Generating foreign keys", and skim the first pages of 5.2 so functional dependencies are not unfamiliar. This one document gives the vocabulary, the discovery-then-selection structure and the tool landscape. VERIFIED: PDF read, quotes on the prior-art page checked against it.

2. Jiang, Naumann. Holistic primary key and foreign key detection. Journal of Intelligent Information Systems 54(3): 439-461, 2020. doi:10.1007/s10844-019-00562-z. Springer paywalled; free PDF: https://hpi.de/oldsite/fileadmin/user_upload/fachgebiete/naumann/publications/PDFs/2020_jiang_holistic.pdf — Sections 2 and 4. The paper closest to what stele's heuristics do. After it you can say "stele's rules are this feature set with hand-set weights" and cite it. VERIFIED: PDF read.

3. Dürsch et al. Inclusion Dependency Discovery: An Experimental Evaluation of Thirteen Algorithms. CIKM 2019, 219-228. doi:10.1145/3357384.3357916. ACM paywalled; free PDF: https://hpi.de/oldsite/fileadmin/user_upload/fachgebiete/naumann/publications/PDFs/2019_duersch_inclusion.pdf — Sections 1 to 3 only, four pages. Hardness, unary versus n-ary, and the algorithm lineage. This is what lets you say why per-candidate SQL is a legitimate strategy and what it costs. VERIFIED: PDF read.

## Canonical, short, expected to know by name

4. Rostin, Albrecht, Bauckmann, Naumann, Leser. A Machine Learning Approach to Foreign Key Discovery. WebDB 2009. https://hpi.de/fileadmin/user_upload/fachgebiete/naumann/publications/PDFs/2009_rostin_a.pdf — Six pages, read it all. The citation for column names being a top feature. VERIFIED: PDF read.

5. Kulkarni, Michels. Temporal features in SQL:2011. SIGMOD Record 41(3), 2012. doi:10.1145/2380776.2380786. https://sigmodrecord.org/publications/sigmodRecord/1209/pdfs/07.industry.kulkarni.pdf — Eight pages. Gives the standard SQL Server temporal tables implement, and the distinction between system-versioned and application-time periods. In those terms stele's _history tables carry application-time periods, which is sharper than saying the engine owns the history. Read before any SQL Server conversation. NOT VERIFIED: cited from the review, PDF not opened.

6. Papenbrock, Kruse, Quiané-Ruiz, Naumann. Divide and Conquer-based Inclusion Dependency Discovery (BINDER). PVLDB 8(7): 774-785, 2015. http://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol8/p774-papenbrock.pdf — Skim. The exact-IND algorithm both Metanome and Desbordante ship. NOT VERIFIED beyond the URL.

7. Zhang, Hadjieleftheriou, Ooi, Procopiuc, Srivastava. On Multi-Column Foreign Key Discovery. PVLDB 3(1): 805-814, 2010. doi:10.14778/1920841.1920944 — Abstract and section 2. The randomness criterion: foreign key values look like a random sample of the primary key's. NOT VERIFIED: DOI from search, no PDF fetched.

8. Su, Wang, Tan, Ma, PVLDB 18(4), 2024 — already cited on the page. Read section 2 for the definitions. VERIFIED.

9. Kimball Group. Slowly Changing Dimensions. https://www.kimballgroup.com/2008/08/slowly-changing-dimensions/ — Free substitute for the SCD chapter of The Data Warehouse Toolkit. Part 2, which covers type 2, is a separate post. PARTIALLY VERIFIED: part 1 fetched, part 2 not.

## Only if going deeper

10. Chen, Narasayya, Chaudhuri. Fast Foreign-Key Detection in Microsoft SQL Server PowerPivot for Excel. PVLDB 7(13): 1417-1428, 2014. https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/04/FKPowerPivot.pdf — The closest published analogue to a product using heuristics and pruning rather than full discovery, under an interactive time budget. NOT VERIFIED.

11. Kruse, Naumann. Efficient Discovery of Approximate Dependencies (Pyro). PVLDB 11(7), 2018. https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol11/p759-kruse.pdf — Sampling to hypothesise, full data to confirm. Relevant to how --sample is used. NOT VERIFIED.

12. Snodgrass. Developing Time-Oriented Database Applications in SQL. Morgan Kaufmann 2000. Free from the author: https://www2.cs.arizona.edu/~rts/tdbbook.pdf — Valid-time predicates and half-open intervals, the background for valid_at and overlaps. NOT VERIFIED.

13. Abedjan, Golab, Naumann, Papenbrock. Data Profiling. Synthesis Lectures on Data Management, 2018. doi:10.1007/978-3-031-01865-7. Paywalled. A superset of item 1; only if you want the book.

14. Rahm, Bernstein. A survey of approaches to automatic schema matching. The VLDB Journal 10: 334-350, 2001. Paywalled; the 2011 follow-up is free at https://vldb.org/pvldb/vol4/p695-bernstein_madhavan_rahm.pdf — Only to place name heuristics in the schema-matching taxonomy. In that taxonomy stele's name rules are an element-level schema-based name matcher, and its containment check is an instance-level matcher. Useful framing for a talk, not for the docs.

15. Kivinen, Mannila. Approximate inference of functional dependencies from relations. Theoretical Computer Science 149(1): 129-149, 1995. Paywalled. Origin of the g3 error measure, only to know where the name comes from.

## Do not chase

Bell and Brockhausen 1995 is an ML-Net workshop paper; cite it through Dürsch, which describes it. Papenbrock and Naumann, Data-driven Schema Normalization, EDBT 2017, is where the primary key features originate; cited via the Jiang and Naumann bibliography.

## Current direction, if someone raises it

Two 2026 preprints a researcher may bring up: Cong et al., Nexus: Inferring Join Graphs from Metadata Alone via Iterative Low-Rank Matrix Completion, arXiv:2602.08186 — join inference from metadata alone, motivated by settings where access to data values is constrained, which is stele's constraint; and Tang et al., LLM-FK: Multi-Agent LLM Reasoning for Foreign Key Detection, arXiv:2603.07278. NOT VERIFIED beyond abstracts.

title: Replica DDL emits IDENTITY on integer primary keys
description:
Every single-column integer primary key compiles with `IDENTITY` in the replica DDL, because `mapped_column(BigInteger(), primary_key=True)` leaves `autoincrement="auto"`.

```
[H3WidgetId] BIGINT NOT NULL IDENTITY,
```

The replica mirrors data whose keys are owned upstream, so the column must carry the source's values. ORM loads happen to work, since SQLAlchemy's mssql dialect toggles `IDENTITY_INSERT` for them. A bulk load - `bcp`, `BULK INSERT`, most ETL tools - without `KEEPIDENTITY` silently assigns new keys and breaks every foreign key pointing at the table. Wrong data, no error.

The sample DDL in `docs/pipeline/ddl-and-check.md` shows no `IDENTITY`, so the documented intent already disagrees with the output.

## Direction

Emit `autoincrement=False` on primary key columns. In this tool's domain the keys are always upstream-owned, so there is no case where the database should be assigning them.

## Done when

Generated primary keys carry `autoincrement=False`, the replica DDL contains no `IDENTITY`, and a test asserts it on an integer key.
close_reason: Primary key columns carry autoincrement=False, so the replica DDL declares no IDENTITY. Fixed in the template; the rule is unconditional so the generator needed no branch. Landed in its own pull request; the closure rides here because ticket bookkeeping was kept to one process.

title: Reconcile how the CLI resolves Databricks connection settings from the environment
description:
## What prompted this

Connection settings exported in a zsh session were not picked up by `stele introspect`, and the run only succeeded once `--host`, `--http-path`, and `--token` were passed explicitly.

**The cause of that particular run is not established.** Reading the three documented variables works. Exercising `cli._engine` with `databricks_engine` patched out, `DATABRICKS_SERVER_HOSTNAME`, `DATABRICKS_HTTP_PATH`, and `DATABRICKS_TOKEN` all resolve; the hostname has `https://` and a trailing slash stripped; and a flag overrides its matching variable without discarding the other two. Two explanations remain and neither is confirmed:

- `DATABRICKS_HOST` was set rather than `DATABRICKS_SERVER_HOSTNAME`. The Databricks CLI and the Databricks SDK use the first name. `databricks-sql-connector`, whose naming stele follows, uses the second. stele ignores the first entirely.
- The assignments lacked `export`, leaving them as zsh parameters that no child process inherits.

`env | grep DATABRICKS` in that shell would separate the two. That is worth knowing, but it is not a prerequisite for this ticket: each defect below was reproduced on its own and stands whether or not any of them explains that run.

## Defects

**`DATABRICKS_HOST` is ignored.** Someone arriving from `databricks configure` or the SDK already has it exported, and stele reports the connection settings as missing while a usable hostname sits in the environment.

**The missing-configuration path prints a traceback.** With nothing set, `stele introspect` raises `RuntimeError` out of `DatabricksConfig.from_env` and the user gets a Python stack trace. The other missing-value path in `cli._engine` raises `SystemExit` and prints one line. Same failure, two presentations, and the traceback is the one a first-time user hits.

**`DATABRICKS_CATALOG` and `DATABRICKS_SCHEMA` cannot be reached from the CLI.** `DatabricksConfig.from_env` reads both, but `cli._engine` calls `from_env` only when `DATABRICKS_SERVER_HOSTNAME` is unset, and `from_env` raises unconditionally in exactly that case. Confirmed by probe: with `DATABRICKS_CATALOG` set, the resolved catalog is still the `--catalog` value. Since `--catalog` is `required=True` on `introspect`, `profile`, and `infer`, no invocation reaches either variable. `from_env` has no successful path from the CLI at all; it only ever raises.

**There is no file-based source.** Every setting is read from `os.environ` and nothing else. `.env` and `.envrc` are gitignored, but no code reads either. A setting that lives only in a shell session does not survive a second terminal, a new day, or an assignment made without `export` — the last being one of the two unconfirmed causes of the run above.

## Direction

**Two names, canonical first.** `DATABRICKS_SERVER_HOSTNAME` is read first and `DATABRICKS_HOST` is a fallback. The alias is what someone arriving from `databricks configure` or the SDK already has exported, and it usually carries a full `https://` URL, which the existing normalization already strips.

**A project-local `.env`.** Reading one removes the whole class of settings that never reach the process, and keeps a token out of shell history and out of `~/.zshrc`. Take `python-dotenv` as a core dependency rather than parsing the file here: `export` prefixes, quoting, escapes, and multi-line values have enough edge cases to be worth not owning, and it is pure Python with no dependencies of its own. Load once in `main()` before argparse dispatch, with `override=False`, searching upward from the working directory so an invocation from a subdirectory still finds the file at the project root.

**Precedence is one sentence: flag, then exported environment, then `.env`.** An exported variable beating the file is the right direction; it is the one just typed.

**`~/.databrickscfg` is out of scope.** It is the file someone arriving from `databricks configure` actually has, but reading it correctly means profiles, which means depending on `databricks-sdk`. That is too large a dependency for the convenience.

A file source raises the stakes on the catalog and schema defect rather than lowering them. Someone writing a `.env` will put a catalog in it, and it stays unreachable while `--catalog` is `required=True`. Make the two variables work rather than deleting them from `from_env`.

## Done when

`DATABRICKS_HOST` resolves as a fallback for `DATABRICKS_SERVER_HOSTNAME`; a `.env` file is loaded with flag, exported environment, then file precedence; missing configuration exits with a single readable message naming all three sources rather than a traceback; and `DATABRICKS_CATALOG` and `DATABRICKS_SCHEMA` are reachable from the CLI.
close_reason: DATABRICKS_HOST reads as a fallback for DATABRICKS_SERVER_HOSTNAME; a project-local .env is loaded with flag > exported environment > file precedence; missing settings exit with one line naming all three sources; --catalog is optional so DATABRICKS_CATALOG and DATABRICKS_SCHEMA are reachable.
